text: An index is a real database structure that speeds up queries filtered or sorted on specific fields. This lesson covers what an index actually is, its real cost, where it lives in ServiceNow, and how to decide which fields actually deserve one.

Underneath every ServiceNow table is a real relational database. Find a record by its unique ID, and the database jumps straight to it. But ask for every record where assignment_group equals Network Ops, and without help, the database has only one option: check every single row, one at a time, to see if it matches.

An index is a separate structure the database maintains alongside the table, built on specific fields, that lets it find matching rows directly instead of checking every row. It's the same idea as a book's index letting you jump straight to a page instead of reading the whole book looking for a word.

But an index is not a free performance upgrade. Every time a record is inserted or updated, the database has to update every index that covers the fields that changed, so the index stays accurate. More indexes on a table means more work on every single write, whether or not those indexes are actually used by a query. Indexes also consume real storage.

This isn't a hidden database-administrator setting. Indexing ties directly to the table's Dictionary — the same Dictionary Entries you used earlier in this path to define a field's type and validation. A field gets configured as indexed at the dictionary level, table by table, field by field.

The real guidance: index fields that actually show up in your Encoded Query conditions and sort orders from courses 2 and 3 — the field=value conditions behind every list filter, report, and addQuery call — especially on large tables. A field nobody filters or sorts on gains nothing from being indexed. It just adds write overhead with no matching read benefit, which is why indexing everything is a real, common mistake.

Indexes trade write cost for read speed, configured through the Dictionary, and only worth it on fields genuinely used in filters and sorts. Next up: query-plan basics, and how to tell whether a slow query is actually using the index you've set up.
